comparator.name: Rechtsgeleerdheid (Dutch Law)
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 regulations describe a three-year, 180 EC Dutch Law degree. Students build on introductory law courses to enter later semesters. Legal and professional skills run alongside the law courses. The final year includes 12 EC of electives and an 18 EC thesis sequence, with 3 EC of research methods and 15 EC for the individual thesis. The public curriculum page also previews a separate 2027–2028 plan.
components: Introduction to the Foundations of Law; year 1, semester 1
Introduction to Private Law; year 1, semester 1
Introduction to Administrative Law; year 1, semester 1
Introduction to Tax Law; year 1, semester 1
Introduction to Constitutional Law; year 1, semester 2
Introduction to International and European Law; year 1, semester 2
Introduction to Criminal Law and Criminal Procedure; year 1, semester 2
International and European Law; year 2, semester 3
Constitutional and Administrative Law; year 2, semester 3
Company and Insolvency Law; year 2, semester 4
Marital Property and Succession Law; year 2, semester 4
Criminal Law and Criminal Procedure; year 3, semester 5

Open elective space, year 3 semester 6: a legal internship, courses at another faculty, law courses at the faculty, an approved individual project (maximum 6 EC) or MaRBLe, within the Regeling Keuzeonderwijs
Eindwerkstuk (bachelor thesis, including 3 EC research methods; LAW3501)
Bachelor thesis; 3 EC in semester 5 and 15 EC in semester 6, of which 3 EC research methods and 15 EC the individual thesis

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Private and commercial law: the law of persons and relationships, obligations (contract and tort), property, company and insolvency law, succession and private international law, and the supervisory civil procedure; the programme introduces private law in year 1 and deepens it in years 2 and 3

Constitutional and administrative law, with administrative procedure, tax law and employment law as related public-law fields: the principles of the Dutch state, the powers of government and the legal protection of citizens, taught in an introduction in year 1 and the integrated course Staats- en Bestuursrecht in year 2
Criminal law and criminal procedure, introduced in year 1 and deepened in year 3 (Straf- en Strafprocesrecht)
International and European law: an introduction in year 1 and the course Internationaal en Europees Recht in year 2, with private international law

Foundations of law: the introductory and year-3 courses Grondslagen van het Recht, which the final qualifications describe as historical, philosophical, legal-theoretical and psychological perspectives on law

Legal reasoning, argumentation and legal skills: logic and interpretation methods, building and defending a legal argument, changing position and presenting the counter-argument, written and oral communication, taught through the Juridische Vaardigheden courses and problem-based small-group education, with simulated court proceedings

Legal research and research methods: the bachelor thesis (Eindwerkstuk, 18 EC, including 3 EC of research methods and a research proposal) and the final qualification of independently writing a substantial scientific paper and collecting, assessing and processing legislation, case law and literature

The relationship of law to non-legal disciplines: the final qualifications name criminology, psychology, political science, economics, sociology, informatics and technology and religious studies as disciplines whose relationship to law students must understand and whose contribution to solving a legal problem they must be able to describe
adjacent: Law and social problems: the programme teaches which legal fields address which specific contemporary social questions, and applies legal principles to current social issues
questions: How does law shape everyday life, and how do different legal fields address contemporary social problems?

trace: analyses the economic and social impact of AI, including inequality, AI governance and ethics, corporate governance and regulation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the regulation of technology as a current social issue

Studies comparative contract law, cross-border sales and services, trade finance, intellectual property and commercial dispute resolution, including arbitration. It covers employment in international business without matching a Dutch employment law module.

analyses taxation, public spending, redistribution and the role of government in the economy; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the economics of taxation behind tax law but does not teach tax law

teaches how a new venture is formed, validated and planned and is the formal prerequisite of Transnational Business Law; it makes a specific complementary contribution only as the business-organisation background to company and business law and teaches no legal content

teaches research design, sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the research-methods training embedded in the bachelor thesis, although it is empirical rather than doctrinal legal research

examines AI fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility and accountability; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the relationship between technology and law and to the contemporary social issues that regulation of AI addresses

examines how governance structures, laws and institutions shape decisions on water safety and land use in a Dutch delta region; it makes a specific complementary contribution to how public law responds to a concrete social and environmental problem

examines how sustainability policy is made and enforced at local, national and international level and which actors shape it; it makes a specific complementary contribution to public regulation as a response to social problems

teaches the drivers and societal impacts of climate change (including migration), climate governance and climate justice; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the climate and sustainability questions that legal fields address
trains the recognition of misleading claims and the critical evaluation of arguments and evidence; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the critical analysis and assessment of arguments

gives the legal, social and normative perspectives on law, compares legal systems, surveys constitutional, administrative, criminal, international and human-rights law and selected private law, and trains case-law reading and trial simulation; it directly implements the foundations of law and the broad introduction to the principal fields of law

examines gendered histories of slavery, marginalisation and community activism in the United States; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the history of discrimination and rights movements as social problems that legal fields address

teaches human rights as positive law (treaties, monitoring mechanisms, case law) together with their historical and natural-law philosophical foundations; it directly implements the philosophical and historical perspective on law and the human-rights part of international and European law

teaches criminal accountability, justification and excuse, the legality principle, the presumption of innocence and the justification of punishment, with case-law analysis and a simulated legal aid clinic; it directly implements substantive criminal law and the skill of formulating a normative legal opinion, although criminal procedure is not taught as a separate subject

teaches the sources, subjects and organisation of public international law and its domains (use of force, armed conflict, international criminal law, refugee and environmental law); it directly implements international law
Studies constitutions, legislatures, rights and judicial review across systems and introduces administrative remedies, participation, procedural fairness and discretion.

teaches property, tort and contract law with a comparative approach (Germany, France, England, China, the United States); it directly implements the core of private law, although not Dutch law specifically

teaches the institutional framework of the EU, fundamental rights, citizenship and the free movement of persons, workers, goods and establishment, with a problem-based case study; it directly implements European law

introduces the central themes of Western philosophy and trains critical reasoning and the articulation of arguments, with explicit links to law; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the philosophical perspective on law and to legal argumentation

teaches theories of moral reasoning (virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism), responsibility and the practical ethics of equality and historical injustice; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the philosophical foundations of law and to the normative argumentation that criminal and human-rights law rely on

examines how influential political theories justify the existence and organisation of political power; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the theoretical foundations of the state on which constitutional law rests

teaches the structures, institutions and functioning of political systems and democracies with the methods of political science; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the political-science context of constitutional and administrative law and to the relationship between law and political science

teaches the schools of international-relations theory and ends with a United Nations Security Council simulation; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the political theory of the international system in which public international law operates

teaches the actors, institutions and decision-making rules of the European Union and how its policies are made; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the political context in which European law is created

studies conflict and peacebuilding through history, sociology, political science and law and compares legal and non-legal conceptions of justice and reconciliation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the international-law domains of armed conflict and international criminal law

introduces sociological concepts, methods and theories of how institutions and societies work; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the sociological perspective on law and to the relationship between sociology and law
teaches the design, data collection, analysis and reporting of qualitative research; it makes a specific complementary contribution to studying how social problems are experienced and addressed

examines leading social theories and debates about modernity, including colonial responses; it makes a specific complementary contribution as the social theory behind the social problems that legal fields address

teaches social-movement theory and environmental justice with case studies; it makes a specific complementary contribution to how legal and non-legal actors address environmental injustice as a social problem
examines civil society, solidarity, the public sphere and civil repair in modern societies; it makes a specific complementary contribution to how societies respond to social problems beyond the law

combines psychology and social science in an international research project on young people's resilience to radicalisation through democratic school culture and civic engagement; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the psychological and social perspective on extremism, which criminal law addresses

trains the construction and delivery of persuasive arguments, with classical rhetorical theory; it makes a specific complementary contribution to communicating legal arguments clearly and persuasively

trains public speaking and debating through practice-based exercises; it makes a specific complementary contribution to oral argument and debate, which the programme practises in simulated court proceedings

builds on rhetoric and argumentation theory to analyse persuasion in domains including law, with framing and the ethics of persuasion; it makes a specific complementary contribution to building and presenting legal arguments

examines how media support or resist systemic racism, power and injustice from the late nineteenth century to the present; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the racial-justice problems that human-rights and criminal-justice law address

alternatives.label: Legal Studies, Politics and Argumentation
alternatives.labelReason: Study private law, criminal justice, constitutional and administrative law, and international and European law in comparative and international settings. Use politics and philosophy to understand legal institutions and develop arguments through rhetoric and debate. Maastricht offers a fuller sequence in Dutch law, procedure and legal research.
alternatives.concept: Study private law, criminal justice, constitutional and administrative law, and international and European law in comparative and international settings. Use politics and philosophy to understand legal institutions and develop arguments through rhetoric and debate. Maastricht offers a fuller sequence in Dutch law, procedure and legal research.
progression: Law, Society & Justice precedes the specialist law courses. The entrepreneurship gateway precedes Transnational Business Law, and Research Methods & Statistics precedes Public Economics. Introductory rhetoric precedes persuasion and community debate. Comparative politics precedes European Union Politics.

alternatives.label: Law and Society
alternatives.labelReason: Explore how legal rules shape daily life and how societies respond to problems involving rights, crime, discrimination, the environment and technology. Combine comparative law with sociology, ethics and qualitative research. Use case studies in areas such as water governance, environmental justice and AI regulation.
alternatives.concept: Explore how legal rules shape daily life and how societies respond to problems involving rights, crime, discrimination, the environment and technology. Combine comparative law with sociology, ethics and qualitative research. Use case studies in areas such as water governance, environmental justice and AI regulation.
progression: Law, Society & Justice precedes the specialist law courses. Introductory sociology precedes modern and contemporary social theory and qualitative methods. Climate Change precedes water and sustainability governance. The foundations in law and sociology precede the third-year work on media, justice and youth resilience.
alternatives.distinctness: The plans share seven law courses and five other courses. Law and Society develops qualitative research and social theory and uses them to investigate environmental justice, technology governance, media and race, gender and youth extremism. The closest plan develops commercial law, political institutions and argumentation. Each plan has twelve courses, or 90 EC, unique to it.
traceOverrides: gives the legal, social and normative perspectives on law and explicitly examines the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice; it directly implements the legal and social view of law that organises this alternative

teaches human rights as positive law and as historical and philosophical claims about liberty and equality, with landmark cases on contentious politicised disputes; it directly implements how a legal field addresses social problems of rights and inequality

teaches criminal accountability, the justification of punishment and recent developments in criminal law, with interdisciplinary research into organised crime and a simulated legal aid clinic; it directly implements how criminal law and criminal justice address crime as a social problem
Examines treaties, jurisdiction, rights, conflict and the environment through public international law. These topics illustrate how law responds to cross-border problems.

teaches constitutional and administrative law, including the guarantee of rights, restrictions on government power and judicial review; it directly implements how public law protects individuals and sets limits on government

opens from the everyday situations (home, neighbours, transactions) in which private law determines rights and obligations and uncovers the social, economic and political pressures behind legal principles; it directly implements how private law shapes everyday life
Examines EU institutions, rights, citizenship, free movement and regulation, showing how EU law affects people and businesses.

introduces sociological concepts, methods and theories for understanding societies from everyday interaction to global phenomena; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the sociological analysis of the social problems legal fields address

teaches moral reasoning and practical ethics (equality, poverty and wealth, climate change, historical injustice); it makes a specific complementary contribution to the normative questions raised when law is applied to current social issues

teaches how political systems and democracies function and why citizens grow dissatisfied with them; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the political context of the social problems public law responds to

studies the causes of and responses to violent and non-violent conflict and compares how justice, truth and reconciliation are mobilised in legal and non-legal settings; it makes a specific complementary contribution to how law responds to conflict as a social problem

candidates.label: Law in society: legal fields addressing social problems and current social issues

selection.assessment: The closest plan covers the broad legal core with comparative law, private and commercial law, legal reasoning and related skills. Law and Society develops the programme interests in everyday law, legal responses to social problems and applying principles to current issues. Each plan has 90 EC of courses that the other lacks. A separate criminal-law direction could use criminal accountability and organised crime, with social context from youth resilience and media coverage of crime. UCR has limited depth in criminal procedure and no dedicated follow-on criminal-law course. A separate international and European law direction could draw on trade governance, European politics, conflict and international relations. The closest plan already covers the three main overlapping law courses and the institutional context. The additional courses develop international politics or trade, with limited additional legal depth. The two options therefore retain the relevant criminal and international courses within their broader curricula.

blocks: Both introduce legal traditions and ways of thinking about law. UCR also examines law as a social institution.
Both draw on history and philosophy. UCR focuses on the foundations of human rights. Maastricht also covers legal theory and the psychology of law.
Both introduce private law. UCR uses comparative examples in property, tort and contract. Maastricht introduces the Dutch system of private rights and obligations.
Both study contracts and remedies. UCR focuses on cross-border commercial transactions and arbitration. Maastricht studies Dutch obligations more broadly, including tort and unjust enrichment.
Maastricht studies jurisdiction and choice of law in cross-border private disputes. UCR covers related commercial disputes within Transnational Business Law.
UCR studies property within Principles of Private Law. Maastricht provides a separate course.
Maastricht provides dedicated study of Dutch company and insolvency law.
Maastricht provides a dedicated course on property between partners and succession.
Maastricht provides a dedicated Dutch employment law course. UCR addresses employment in the context of transnational business.
Maastricht provides a dedicated course on Dutch civil procedure.
Both study limits on government power, rights and judicial review. UCR compares legal systems and covers administrative law within that comparison.
UCR covers public authority and administrative remedies within comparative constitutional law.
UCR covers this area within Comparative Constitutional Law, paired below with Maastricht’s combined constitutional and administrative law course.
Maastricht provides a separate course on administrative procedure. UCR covers administrative remedies and procedural fairness within Comparative Constitutional Law.
Public Economics covers taxation and redistribution. Maastricht studies tax law.
Both study criminal liability and the principles of criminal law. Maastricht also introduces criminal procedure.
Maastricht extends the study of criminal law and criminal procedure in Year 3. UCR covers core criminal law in a single course.
Both introduce the sources and subjects of international law. Maastricht also introduces EU law in this course.
UCR examines EU institutions, competences, legal sources and enforcement. Maastricht combines EU law with further study of public international law.
Both develop first-year academic and professional skills. Maastricht includes coaching and portfolio work across a three-year sequence.
Maastricht trains students to read legal sources and reason through Dutch legal problems. UCR develops related argument skills across several courses.
Maastricht continues training in legal argument and interpretation of Dutch legal sources.
Maastricht has a further module in practical legal skills.
Maastricht continues its coached professional skills sequence in Year 2.
Maastricht completes its professional skills sequence in Year 3.
Students can use the final 12 EC for an internship, faculty or external courses, or an approved project or research option.
Maastricht requires a research proposal and an individual thesis. UCR methods courses develop empirical research skills, and optional independent research sits outside the scheduled courses.

notes.text: Maastricht builds depth in Dutch private, public and criminal law and legal procedure over three years. UCR offers a comparative introduction to several legal fields and uses politics, philosophy and sociology to examine how legal institutions work.

Maastricht requires a legal skills sequence and an individual thesis. The 12 EC of final-semester electives can include a legal internship. UCR’s optional independent research is separate from the scheduled coursework.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Dutch Law bachelor teaches the main fields of Dutch law through legal problems and small-group work. Students also study European and international law and complete an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The comparison uses the 2026–2027 curriculum. One UCR plan combines comparative law with politics and argumentation. The other studies how law relates to social issues. Maastricht provides a fuller sequence in Dutch law and legal practice.
